claims.text: Rapid cooling during synthesis promotes atomic-scale homogeneity in noble metal–based high-entropy alloy nanomaterials.
Greater atomic-scale homogeneity leads to enhanced catalytic performance.
Slow cooling allows greater phase segregation than rapid cooling.
Rapid cooling freezes the atomic configuration induced by high configurational entropy.
Freezing the atomic configuration prevents phase segregation.
A homogeneous atomic distribution increases the density of effective catalytic active sites.
Beneficial electronic interactions among the noble metals increase catalytic active-site effectiveness.
Rapidly cooled nanomaterials will have higher reaction rates or turnover frequencies than compositionally identical, slowly cooled nanomaterials.
Phase segregation in slowly cooled materials may reduce catalytic active-site effectiveness.
Slowly cooled alloy nanomaterials are expected to exhibit lower catalytic activity because they contain more phase segregation.
The proposed effect requires synthesis temperatures high enough to promote atomic diffusion and a process in which rapid quenching is feasible.
The proposed effect is relevant to catalytic processes governed by the density and nature of active sites.
The hypothesis may not apply to low-temperature synthesis regimes or systems in which factors other than active-site density and nature dominate catalytic behavior.
The magnitude of the rapid-cooling benefit may depend on alloy composition and reaction conditions.
